power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain.

We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures.
Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging.

Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients (β = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 -1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants (β = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 -0.38).
No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis.
In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram (β = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 -1.61).
IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment.
These findings support astroglial involvement in MDD and link peripheral immune variation to subcortical brain structure.
IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.

text.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a clinically and biologically heterogeneous disorder for which current diagnostic categories provide little information about underlying pathophysiology or treatment outcome.

This heterogeneity has constrained biomarker discovery and may explain why inflammatory, neuroimaging, and molecular measures frequently distinguish patients from healthy individuals at the group level, yet rarely achieve individual-level specificity (Abi-Dargham et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This heterogeneity has constrained biomarker discovery and may explain why inflammatory, neuroimaging, and molecular measures frequently distinguish patients from healthy individuals at the group level, yet rarely achieve individual-level specificity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abi-Dargham et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Next to the assessment of group differences in biomarkers of MDD, mapping relationships between immune profiles, clinical, and neurobiological measures may clarify how different pathophysiological processes interlock in depression and lead to the development of more effective stratification methods for targeted interventions.
Substantial evidence implicates immune dysregulation in MDD.

Meta-analyses have identified higher circulating C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin (IL)-6, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and related inflammatory mediators in depression (Köhler et al., 2018; Osimo et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses have identified higher circulating C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin (IL)-6, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and related inflammatory mediators in depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Köhler et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Osimo et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, translocator protein positron emission tomography (PET) studies show altered neuroimmune activity in corticolimbic regions (De Picker et al., 2023; Eggerstorfer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, translocator protein positron emission tomography (PET) studies show altered neuroimmune activity in corticolimbic regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(De Picker et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Eggerstorfer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal studies further suggest bidirectional associations between inflammation and depression: higher CRP and IL-6 predict subsequent depressive symptoms, while depression may itself contribute to later increases in these markers (Colasanto et al., 2020; Mac Giollabhui et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Longitudinal studies further suggest bidirectional associations between inflammation and depression: higher CRP and IL-6 predict subsequent depressive symptoms, while depression may itself contribute to later increases in these markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Colasanto et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Mac Giollabhui et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Immune alterations may therefore contribute to depressive pathophysiology while also being reinforced by the course and consequences of illness.
Immune involvement is unlikely to be uniform across MDD.

Inflammatory markers have been associated more consistently with anhedonia, fatigue, psychomotor slowing, sleep disturbance, and appetite change than with overall symptom severity (Kofod et al., 2022; Milaneschi et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Inflammatory markers have been associated more consistently with anhedonia, fatigue, psychomotor slowing, sleep disturbance, and appetite change than with overall symptom severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kofod et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Milaneschi et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This has led to proposals for an inflammation-related subtype characterized by elevated inflammatory activity and prominent neurovegetative and reward-related symptoms (Jha et al., 2025; Miller, 2025).
text.formatted: This has led to proposals for an inflammation-related subtype characterized by elevated inflammatory activity and prominent neurovegetative and reward-related symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Jha et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Miller, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Inflammation may also contribute to variation in antidepressant outcomes.
Higher baseline inflammatory activity has been associated with poorer response to standard antidepressants (Bufalino et al., 2013; Carvalho et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Higher baseline inflammatory activity has been associated with poorer response to standard antidepressants <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bufalino et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Carvalho et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: But findings vary across markers and treatments, and changes in inflammatory markers do not necessarily follow symptom improvement (Kofod et al., 2022).
text.formatted: But findings vary across markers and treatments, and changes in inflammatory markers do not necessarily follow symptom improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kofod et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Whether peripheral markers provide information about subsequent treatment outcome beyond their association with diagnostic status or baseline symptom severity therefore remains unresolved.
Understanding how circulating markers relate to brain biology is another key challenge.
Beyond their inflammatory roles, cytokines can modulate synaptic function, with effects that vary across cellular targets and neural circuits (Salvador et al., 2021; Wheeler and Quintana, 2025).
text.formatted: Beyond their inflammatory roles, cytokines can modulate synaptic function, with effects that vary across cellular targets and neural circuits <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Salvador et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wheeler and Quintana, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Peripheral immune signals can influence the central nervous system via endothelial and vagal pathways (Huerta et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2024), changes in the blood-brain barrier (Huang et al., 2021; Tyagi and Bartley, 2026), immune-cell trafficking (Li et al., 2018; Thomson et al., 2020), kynurenine metabolism (Paul et al., 2022; Savitz, 2020), oxidative and nitrosative stress (di Penta et al., 2013), and shifts in glial activity (Miller and Raison, 2016; Shen et al., 2026; Upthegrove et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Peripheral immune signals can influence the central nervous system via endothelial and vagal pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Huerta et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Jin et al., 2024)</ref>, changes in the blood-brain barrier <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Huang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Tyagi and Bartley, 2026)</ref>, immune-cell trafficking <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Li et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Thomson et al., 2020)</ref>, kynurenine metabolism <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Paul et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Savitz, 2020)</ref>, oxidative and nitrosative stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(di Penta et al., 2013)</ref>, and shifts in glial activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Miller and Raison, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Shen et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Upthegrove et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Serotonergic regulation may represent one interface between immune activity and antidepressant response, but direct human evidence linking cytokines to in vivo SERT availability remains limited.

Cytokines may influence serotonergic signaling through tryptophan-kynurenine metabolism, SERT regulation, and neuroplastic pathways (Savitz, 2020; Zhu et al., 2006), while antidepressant treatment has been associated with changes in immune activity (Bleibel et al., 2025; Köhler et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).

text.text: By contrast, peripheral inflammation has been more consistently associated with structural variation in cortical and limbic regions, including the hippocampus, which is sensitive to inflammatory and stress-related processes and may undergo structural changes during antidepressant treatment (Cordero et al., 2026; Evans et al., 2024; Gryglewski et al., 2021; Popovic et al., 2026; Schmaal et al., 2016).
text.formatted: By contrast, peripheral inflammation has been more consistently associated with structural variation in cortical and limbic regions, including the hippocampus, which is sensitive to inflammatory and stress-related processes and may undergo structural changes during antidepressant treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cordero et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Evans et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Gryglewski et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Popovic et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Schmaal et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, immune markers, SERT availability, brain structure, and treatment-related structural change have rarely been examined together.

In the present study, we combined high-sensitivity profiling of circulating immune and glial markers with prospective assessment of antidepressant response, [ 11 C]DASB PET, and structural MRI in a thoroughly characterized case-control cohort.

By evaluating immune associations across complementary clinical and neurobiological phenotypes, we aimed to determine whether immune markers show generalized associations across MDD-related phenotypes or more selective relationships with diagnosis, treatment outcome, serotonergic transmission, or brain structure.

Analyses included 36 patients and 48 healthy controls (Table 1), who were partially used in previous studies by our group (Gryglewski et al., 2019; Klöbl et al., 2025 Klöbl et al., , 2020;; Seiger et al., 2021; Silberbauer et al., 2022; Zadka et al., 2025).

text.text: All participants were non-smokers.
MDD patients were free from antidepressant treatment for at least three months before inclusion and had no comorbid psychiatric or somatic illnesses.

Patients were recruited at the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy at the Medical  (Klöbl et al., 2025 (Klöbl et al., , 2020;; Seiger et al., 2021; Silberbauer et al., 2022; Zadka et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Patients were recruited at the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy at the Medical  <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Klöbl et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Klöbl et al., , 2020;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Seiger et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Silberbauer et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Zadka et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: All participants gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee, conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki, and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02711215).
Venous blood samples were collected during PET/MR scans.
Plasma was separated by centrifugation at 3,506 × g for 4 minutes and stored at -80°C until analysis.
Samples were transported on dry ice and gently thawed on ice immediately before measurement.

Concentrations of inflammatory and neuroglial markers, including interleukins (IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-13, IL-15, IL-17A, IL-22, IL-33), TNF, and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were measured using single-molecule array technology on the SR-X Analyzer platform (Simoa Quanterix, Lexington, MA, USA) (Rissin et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Concentrations of inflammatory and neuroglial markers, including interleukins (IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-13, IL-15, IL-17A, IL-22, IL-33), TNF, and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were measured using single-molecule array technology on the SR-X Analyzer platform (Simoa Quanterix, Lexington, MA, USA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Rissin et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: All analyses were performed by an investigator blinded to clinical data, following the manufacturer's instructions.
Samples and calibrators were equilibrated to room temperature, diluted 1:4 in sample diluent, and measured in duplicate in 96-well plates.
Detector reagent and paramagnetic beads were added sequentially to each well, followed by incubation at 30°C and 800rpm for 30 minutes on a Simoa microplate incubator.
After automated washing with the Simoa microplate washer, streptavidin βgalactosidase was added, and plates were incubated again at 30°C and 800rpm for 10 minutes.
A final wash was followed by drying the plates for 10 minutes before transferring them to the Quanterix SR-X Analyzer for readout.
All assay kits and consumables used are detailed in the supplement and were from the same lot where applicable.
To reduce inter-assay variability, all samples from a single participant were processed on the same plate.
Duplicate measurements underwent quality control as described in the supplementary methods.
IL-17A was designated as an exploratory binary detectable marker because its detection rate was below 80% during replicate quality control.
Analyses were performed in R 4.5.3.
Continuous variables were inspected using histograms and summary statistics, and skewed variables were log-transformed where appropriate.
Immune markers and imaging measures were standardized before analysis.
Continuous covariates were mean-centered within the corresponding analysis dataset.

Associations of plasma marker levels were evaluated across six prespecified analysis domains spanning three broader outcome categories: A) Clinical characteristics (MDD diagnosis, antidepressant response); B) Brain serotonergic transmission (baseline PET serotonin transporter binding potential); and C) Brain structure (baseline subcortical volume, baseline cortical thickness, and longitudinal hippocampal change with treatment).
Models were fitted separately for each immune marker using marker-specific complete cases.
Linear mixed-effects models with participant-specific random intercepts were used for analysis of repeated (regional or longitudinal) measurements.
A) Associations with MDD diagnosis were evaluated using linear regression with immune marker as the outcome and diagnostic group as the predictor.
Antidepressant response was assessed using linear mixed-effects models of MADRS scores measured at baseline and after six weeks of treatment.

text.text: In this multimodal study, we evaluated associations among high-sensitivity plasma immune markers, clinical characteristics, brain serotonergic transmission, and brain structure in individuals with MDD and healthy controls.
Higher baseline IL-13 was associated with greater improvement in depressive symptoms during six weeks of SSRI treatment.
This association survived correction across all primary tests, remained evident after covariate adjustment, and was directionally concordant across secondary symptom measures.
Higher IL-15 showed a similar but nominal association with treatment response.
Moreover, higher baseline IL-13 and IL-15 were both nominally associated with a more positive hippocampal volume change, although these associations did not survive FDR correction.
GFAP concentrations were higher in MDD, and IL-33 was associated with greater subcortical volume at the domain-specific FDR level.
No plasma marker was significantly associated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after multiple-testing correction.
Baseline imaging measures did not differ by diagnosis, and diagnosis did not moderate immune-brain associations.

Xu et al., 2023).

Circulating GFAP should also be interpreted as a nonspecific indicator of altered astroglial integrity or turnover rather than as direct evidence of astrogliosis or neurodegeneration.

However, studies linking GFAP to astrocytic mitochondrial regulation and disrupted astrocyte-serotonin signaling to depression-related behavioral and synaptic abnormalities support the role of astroglial dysfunction in MDD (González-Arias et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025).

text.text: Collectively, these findings point to subtle and heterogeneous astroglial and immune alterations rather than a uniform inflammatory phenotype in MDD.
The strongest evidence concerned antidepressant response: higher IL-13 was associated with greater symptom improvement but not significantly related to baseline severity.
IL-15 showed a similar nominal association, attenuated after covariate adjustment.
Higher concentrations of both cytokines were also associated with greater increases in hippocampal volume during treatment.
Importantly, greater improvement in MADRS was moderately correlated with a more positive change in hippocampal volume.

The clinical and structural findings were therefore linked within individuals, rather than merely parallel, suggesting that IL-13 and IL-15 may index a broader treatment-responsiveness phenotype involving both symptomatic and hippocampal adaptation.

Previous findings support this paired signal: responders had higher pretreatment IL-13 and IL-15 concentrations than nonresponders, although neither cytokine alone showed strong discriminatory ability (Y. Xu et al., 2023).

Diagnosis was confirmed using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I disorders (SCID-I).
Depression severity was assessed using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), Hamilton Rating Scale for depression 17-item (HDRS17), and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI).
Participants underwent baseline [ 11 C]DASB PET/MR scans to measure SERT binding potential (BPP) and brain structure, as in our previous work (see supplement).

Patients then received open-label antidepressant treatment starting with escitalopram 10 mg/day and biweekly follow-up for three months, allowing dose escalation or medication switch in case of non-response or intolerance.
Patients underwent an additional MRI scan 12 weeks after treatment initiation.
Further treatment details are reported elsewhere prospective clinical outcomes assessed at an unmedicated baseline, molecular imaging using [ 11 C]DASB PET, and structural MRI within a single cohort.
The MDD and healthy control groups were well matched.
The young, physically healthy, normal-weight MDD cohort minimizes major confounders in peripheral immune analyses, including obesity, metabolic diseases, comorbidities, and concomitant medication.
At the same time, this selectivity limits generalizability.

Given the cohort's mean age of 28.2 years, BMI of approximately 23, low CRP levels, and the absence of relevant somatic and psychiatric comorbidities, these findings may primarily reflect immunebrain relationships in a low-inflammatory MDD population, rather than in more heterogeneous clinical samples.
Additional limitations include small, modality-dependent sample sizes, and the absence of peripheral immune measurements at follow-up.
Peripheral marker concentrations may not reflect signaling within the central nervous system, while PET binding and structural MRI remain indirect and biologically nonspecific measures.
The observational design precludes causal inference, and the open-label treatment design cannot distinguish general prognostic associations from effects specific to antidepressant treatment.
Taken together, our findings support domain-specific immune associations instead of a unitary inflammatory signature of MDD.
GFAP indicated astroglial alteration, IL-13 emerged as a candidate prognostic marker of treatment response, and IL-33 was associated with subcortical volume.

Overall, peripheral immune variation appeared more closely related to dynamic treatment phenotypes than to static serotonergic or structural brain measures, as further suggested by the exploratory convergence of IL-13 and IL-15 across changes in symptoms and hippocampal volume.

These findings provide a focused framework for prospective studies testing whether peripheral immune profiles can predict and potentially shape clinical and structural adaptation during antidepressant treatment.
